metadata.title: Income inequality is associated with heightened test anxiety and lower academic achievement: A cross-national study in 51 countries

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA 2015 microdata for 15-year-old students across 51 countries. The analytic strategy is a multilevel structural equation modeling approach in Mplus, with income inequality and country affluence at the country level and test anxiety and achievement at the student level, accounting for school-level clustering. The manuscript does not report whether PISA sampling weights (and any replicate-weight scheme) were applied in estimation, nor does it name any weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT). Because the paper does not document weighting, the safest interpretation is that weights were either not applied or not reported; readers should verify in the original Mplus syntax or OECD analysis guidance for PISA 2015.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are Rasch-calibrated test anxiety scores (provided by OECD) and Rasch-modeled achievement scores for reading, mathematics, and science, estimated within OECD’s scaling framework. The paper does not describe how PISA plausible values (PV-based achievement scores) were handled in the multilevel SEM estimation, nor does it report any missing-data procedure for student responses/covariates. This is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically require explicit PV and missing-data handling documentation for reproducibility.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used OECD PISA 2015 data for 15-year-old students from 51 participating countries (including Hong Kong and Chinese Taipei as separate contexts, and B-S-J-G (China) and Spain (Regions) as additional contexts). The manuscript reports the full PISA 2015 student sample size used (389,215) and does not describe additional task/module subsampling or grade/school-type restrictions beyond the PISA 15-year-old target population. No explicit missing-response exclusion rule is reported.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel SEM (Mplus). Model 3: Test anxiety → reading achievement (β = −0.08, p < .001). Model 3: Income inequality → reading achievement (β = −0.15, p = .25). Model 3 mediation (H4): indirect effect = −0.04, p = .55, 90% CI [−0.18, 0.10]. Model 4 moderation (H5): inequality → random-slope predictor for test anxiety → reading (b = 0.03, p = .74). ICC (Model 1 justification): 0.13.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged income inequality (Gini), test anxiety, and student/country covariates (ESCS, gender, and GDP per capita) to predict reading achievement, finding that test anxiety was negatively associated with reading achievement while income inequality had no statistically significant direct effect after covariates. This indicates that reducing students’ test anxiety may be a more actionable lever for reading performance than targeting national income inequality, though the cross-sectional design limits causal claims.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel SEM (Mplus). Model 3: Test anxiety → math achievement (β = −0.10, p < .001). Model 3: Income inequality → math achievement (β = −0.32, p < .001). Model 3 mediation (H4): indirect effect = 0.01, p = .86, 90% CI [−0.16, 0.13]. Model 4 moderation (H5): inequality → random-slope predictor for test anxiety → math (b = 0.04, p = .64). ICC (Model 1 justification): 0.20.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged income inequality (Gini), test anxiety, and student/country covariates (ESCS, gender, and GDP per capita) to predict mathematics achievement, finding that both higher test anxiety and higher income inequality were associated with lower math achievement while the mediation via test anxiety was not significant. This indicates that math-focused supports that reduce anxiety may help, but national inequality alone is unlikely to operate through test anxiety as the sole mechanism, suggesting broader resource and opportunity pathways.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel SEM (Mplus). Model 3: Test anxiety → science achievement (β = −0.10, p < .001). Model 3: Income inequality → science achievement (β = −0.20, p = .13). Model 3 mediation (H4): indirect effect = −0.01, p = .86, 90% CI [−0.17, 0.14]. Model 4 moderation (H5): inequality → random-slope predictor for test anxiety → science (b = 0.22, p = .27). ICC (Model 1 justification): 0.16.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged income inequality (Gini), test anxiety, and student/country covariates (ESCS, gender, and GDP per capita) to predict science achievement, finding that test anxiety was negatively associated with science achievement but income inequality showed no statistically significant direct effect after covariates and did not moderate the anxiety–achievement link. This indicates that classroom- and student-level anxiety interventions may be more relevant for science performance than expecting inequality-driven differences to change how anxiety translates into achievement.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel SEM (Mplus). Model 3: Income inequality → test anxiety (β = 0.67, p < .001). Model 3: SES → test anxiety (β = −0.04, p < .001). Model 3: Gender (male vs female) → test anxiety (β = −0.39, p < .001). Model 3: Country affluence (GDP per capita) → test anxiety (β = 0.10, p = .39). ICC (Model 1 justification): not reported for test anxiety.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 (15-year-olds) the study leveraged income inequality (Gini) and student/country covariates (ESCS, gender, and GDP per capita) to predict test anxiety, finding that higher national income inequality was associated with higher test anxiety even after accounting for socioeconomic status and gender. This indicates that psycho-educational anxiety prevention may be especially important in more unequal societies, while also motivating research into intermediate mechanisms linking macro-inequality to students’ evaluative stress.

data.outcome_summary: This cross-national study analyzed OECD PISA 2015 data for 389,215 fifteen-year-old students across 51 countries to test whether national income inequality (Gini, 2014) is associated with test anxiety and achievement in reading, mathematics, and science. The authors used multilevel SEM in Mplus with random slopes to evaluate direct effects, mediation (test anxiety as mediator), and cross-level moderation (inequality strengthening the anxiety–achievement link), while accounting for school-level clustering. Results showed that income inequality significantly predicted higher test anxiety (β = 0.67, p < .001), and test anxiety significantly predicted lower achievement in all three domains (reading β = −0.08; math β = −0.10; science β = −0.10; all p < .001). Income inequality had a significant negative association with math achievement (β = −0.32, p < .001) but not reading or science after covariates, and mediation/moderation hypotheses were not supported. Limitations include cross-sectional design and incomplete reporting of PV/missing-data handling and survey-weight application, which constrains reproducibility and causal interpretation.
